consequence: Probe and training coefficient ranges agree.

consequence: For a fixed number of gradient examples the original needs ~10x FEWER DISTINCT samples. The paper's 'log2 samples' counts distinct instances, so our per-sample budget is not directly comparable to theirs, and our sample-requirement extrapolations may be pessimistic by up to ~10x.

salsa_2_0: rng.choice(n, h, replace=False) -> exactly h ones

original_salsa: circulant(a) with the strict UPPER TRIANGLE NEGATED, then mod q (i.e. NEGACYCLIC, despite the paper saying 'circulant' and the option being named circ_rlwe)
salsa_2_0: rlwe_variant=circulant (no negation) -- what every completed run used
difference: The original applies a sign flip on wrap-around; our trained runs did not. The original equals the TRANSPOSE of our negacyclic variant.
consequence: The training distribution differs. Row sets are not the same matrices, so the function the model must learn is different, though of the same family and difficulty. Salsa 2.0 implements negacyclic and can select it by config; no completed run used it.

original_salsa: PAPER: gated Universal Transformer, 1024/512, 16-32/4 heads, shared layer looped 2 (enc) and 8 (dec), copy gate, ~51M parameters. SUPPLIED transformer.py: looping and gating DISABLED ('obsolete in Modern SALSA'), plain block stack, RoPE, RMSNorm

original_salsa: specialA = np.identity(N) * K; specialB = inner(specialA, TRUE SECRET). K values include 239145, 42899, Q, 3Q+7, random in [Q,10Q), 71/92/101/193/241

difference: Identical probe geometry. The original builds a target from the true secret (needed only by its batching); ours decodes from <bos> and never constructs one.

original_salsa: write_int takes K mod B^int_len (mod 6561 at base 81), NOT mod q, so a large K can be encoded as a value OUTSIDE Z_q
salsa_2_0: K is reduced mod q, so the probe is always a legal element of Z_q
difference: The original can feed the model values >= q that never occur in training.
consequence: Only K mod q is mathematically meaningful (a.s = K*s_i mod q), so ours is correct. The original's out-of-range probes are an additional, unintended distribution shift on top of the intended one.

difference: The original resolves polarity using the answer it is trying to find.
consequence: The original's reported 'secret matching' figure is optimistic: it takes a max over 6 variants scored against the truth. Ours is a genuine attack statistic. This makes our numbers NOT directly comparable to theirs -- ours are stricter.

original_salsa: success iff any of the 6 variants matches the true secret in ALL N coordinates (np.any(match_counts == N))
salsa_2_0: exact recovery iff candidate == true secret in all n coordinates, plus an explicit all-zeros baseline so sparsity cannot masquerade as recovery
difference: Same all-coordinates criterion; we add the trivial baseline the original does not report.
consequence: None to the criterion. The added baseline prevents a weight-h secret's (n-h)/n free accuracy being read as partial success.
